title: AI ROI calculator: will this workflow pay back this year?
description: Pick one workflow and see the payback month, hours moved to better work and an honest low-to-high range. Sourced defaults, no email needed.
verdict: Subtract review and redo time; vendor calculators often skip it and show bigger savings[^22][^19].
Count about half the freed hours as money, because scattered minutes rarely become output[^1][^21].
Expect a dip first: run costs start in month one while value ramps up[^15][^16].
Buying usually beats building, and a custom build needs high volume to pay back this year[^18][^20].
Time 20 real items before you trust any answer, because self-reported savings run high[^14][^12].

steps: Pick the workflow closest to yours. Its defaults fill in, sized for a firm of 40 to 500 staff, each with a source or marked as our estimate.
Enter your monthly volume. Count 4 weeks of real items if you can.
Check minutes per item and review minutes. Time 20 real items rather than guess.
Enter setup and monthly cost, or start from a typical range. Read the verdict, the range and the input that moves your answer most.
Copy the link to share your inputs, or bring the result to the free diagnostic.
method: Minutes moved per AI item = minutes today, minus review minutes, minus redo rate times minutes today. Review time is the step most calculators skip[^21][^22].
Money per month counts 56% of freed hours: Gartner's example takes a 20% productivity leak, then a 70% harvesting ratio[^1].
Value ramps up over 3 months while run cost starts in month 1, to show the early dip[^15][^16][^25].

Hourly cost is BLS pay times 1.28 to 1.31, the BLS loading for benefits other than paid leave, because pay already includes leave[^5][^6]. Where no single job fits, we use BLS total pay and benefits per hour[^6].

Minutes per item come from MetricNet, APQC and Loopio benchmarks[^7][^9][^11]. Volumes and costs start where a 40 to 500 person firm usually starts, from APQC, IOFM, Loopio and list prices[^9][^26][^28][^30][^32].
Adoption starts at 80%, the active-use rate in the UK government's Copilot trial[^12].
Low and high cases change AI share, review minutes and adoption; payback is not discounted. Above 40% time saved, a reality check appears, since surveyed AI users saved 5.4% of work hours[^13].

summary: An AI ROI calculator asks whether one workflow earns back its setup and running cost. AI drafts the first pass, and people still check each draft[^2][^12]. The answer turns on volume, review minutes and how much freed time becomes real output[^1][^19].
humanRole: A named reviewer checks each AI draft before it goes out, such as the AP clerk, support agent or accountant. The calculator counts that time as a cost[^12][^19].
Exceptions stay with people. Teams where AI took routine items and people reviewed exceptions reported 71% median gains, against 30% where people approved every output[^17].
People decide where freed hours go: faster turnaround, fewer errors, or work that waits today. Early Copilot users spent saved time mostly on focus work[^23].
The ops lead or division head owns the go or no-go call and signs off the spend. Test on timed items first, because many AI projects stop after the proof of concept[^24][^14].

ownData.title: How many items a month does each workflow need to pay back in a year?
ownData.intro: We ran our calculator on each workflow at a volume and on a path typical for a firm of 40 to 500 staff[^9][^28]. We then solved for the monthly volume that pays back within 12 months. Run on 26 Nov 2026.
headers: Volume to pay back in a year: default path / custom build ($80k, then $2,000)

ownData.note: Zavient calculation, 26 Nov 2026: 80% adoption, 56% of hours counted as money, a 3-month ramp, costs from list prices and Forrester[^33][^20]. We left out IT tickets, bank reconciliations and document intake, because at this size they move too few hours to pay for a priced tool[^34][^10][^35]. AI share and review minutes are our assumptions, so change them in the tool.

faq.q: Why is my result lower than vendor ROI calculators show?
faq.a: We subtract the minutes people spend checking AI drafts, the drafts that get redone, and the slow first months[^21][^15]. Some vendor calculators skip these, and one defaults to a 76% resolution rate[^22]. We also count only part of the freed time as money[^1].

faq.q: Why does it show hours moved to better work, not jobs saved?
faq.a: Measured gains are on tasks, not whole roles: 14% more issues resolved per hour in support, and 40% less time on writing tasks[^2][^3]. The hours are real capacity. Your team decides where they go[^23].

faq.q: Where do the default numbers come from?
faq.a: Minutes per item come from APQC, MetricNet and Loopio benchmarks, and volumes and costs from what a 40 to 500 person firm typically has[^9][^7][^11][^26][^30]. Hourly cost is BLS pay plus benefits other than paid leave, which pay already covers[^5][^6]. AI share and review minutes are our estimates, because no neutral benchmark exists.

faq.q: Why does the first month lose money?
faq.a: You pay to run it from day one while people learn the new step[^16]. Research on new technology finds a dip before the gain, and DORA's calculator models one too[^15][^25].

faq.q: How accurate is an AI ROI estimate?
faq.a: Only roughly: an AI ROI estimate is for planning, so the tool shows low, expected and high cases. Self-reported savings run high: developers who felt 20% faster were 19% slower when measured[^14]. Time 20 real items before you decide[^12].

Include one-time setup and monthly running costs: licences or usage fees, upkeep, and the staff time spent checking AI output.[^36][^21] Setup covers configuration, connecting your systems, data clean-up and training, about $14,000 in one Microsoft-funded small-firm study.[^33] AI seats run $21 to $50 a user a month, and most AI projects reviewed on Clutch cost $10,000 to $49,999.[^36][^30][^20]

faq.q: What if it says the workflow doesn't pay back?
faq.a: A no-payback result is still useful: the tool names the most likely lever, such as a cheaper set-up path, more volume, or less review time[^17]. In MIT's study, bought tools succeeded about 67% of the time and internal builds one-third as often[^18]. Bring the numbers to the free 30-minute diagnostic and we will find which lever fits.

faq.q: Why are IT tickets, reconciliations and document intake not in the list?
faq.a: At a firm of 40 to 500 staff they move too few hours to pay for a priced tool. A 150-person firm logs about 200 IT tickets a month, at 1.3 per person[^34][^8], and has about four bank accounts, at 4 hours each[^35][^10]. If yours are bigger, use the blank workflow with your own counts.

pickElse: Software delivery teams: DORA's free calculator models engineering metrics and the early dip in more detail[^25].
Low-volume drafting and meeting notes: turn on AI in tools you already pay for before you price a build[^12][^23].
IT tickets and bank reconciliations at a firm this size: turn on what your software already includes. Too few hours move to justify a project[^34][^35].
Judgment calls with thin data: keep them by hand for now. On tasks outside what AI does well, users were 19 points less likely to be right[^4].
Build cost unknown: price the project first with our AI project cost estimator, then bring the numbers back here[^20].

offer.heading: Not sure this workflow pays back? Get a free diagnostic
offer.body: Want the detailed plan behind your result? Book the free 30-minute diagnostic.

reviews.notes: Wanted a decision line and a range, not one point. Verdict now says this year, next year or year 3, with low, expected and high under it. Fixed: drafting and meeting presets were priced as a $40k build; each workflow now starts from its typical cost path. Fixed (26 Nov): 5 of 8 presets did not pay back on their own defaults; each now starts at a sourced volume for a 40-500 person firm on the path such a firm usually takes, and IT desk, reconciliation and intake were dropped as too small at this size.
Asked what to measure before trusting it. Added 'the number that moves your answer most' and three checks. Fixed: break-even volume now uses the workflow's own unit (invoices, tickets, accounts).

Reads on a phone between meetings. Result sits first, with a sticky verdict bar while editing inputs. Fixed: replaced an FTE-equivalent figure with hours per working day, so it reads as time back, not people.

Controller and head of support wanted their reviewers named. Human-role bullets and preset notes now say who keeps the call. Fixed: reconciliation priced at accountant cost, with the clerk rate noted.

Checked it is not a sales funnel: no email gate, sources on every default, and an honest 'does not pay back' state with cheaper options. Fixed: meeting preset AI share cut to 70% so its default stays inside the measured 2-40% band. Fixed (26 Nov): a no-payback or AI-adds-work result now names the likely lever and links to the free diagnostic.

answers.human-role: Your team stays in charge of reviewing each AI draft, handling exceptions, deciding where freed hours go, and the go or no-go call on spend[^12][^17][^23].
answers.own-data: On the default path, workflows need 110 to 2,200 items a month to pay back in a year, from 110 meetings to 2,200 support tickets. A custom build at $80k needs far more, from 830 meetings to 9,700 invoices a month.
answers.something-else: Pick something else when you run software delivery, draft at low volume, have few IT tickets or reconciliations, face thin-data judgment calls, or haven't priced the build yet[^25][^12][^34][^4][^20].
